subject: languages
title: Memory Management & Garbage Collection
summary: How languages decide where values live and when they die: stack and heap, manual memory and its bugs, reference counting, tracing and generational collectors, modern low-pause GCs in Java and Go, and Rust's ownership and borrowing.

lessons.title: Stack vs heap
lessons.summary: Where values live in C, Python, Java, Go and Rust, why the stack is fast but short-lived, and how escape analysis decides what goes on the heap.
lessons.body:
Every value a program creates has to live somewhere in memory, and sooner or later that memory must be given back. Two common storage mechanisms are the **stack** and the **heap**. Registers, static storage and optimizations also matter; this is an introductory model, not an exhaustive classification.

The difference is about **lifetime**. A conventional call frame is reclaimed on return, while block-scoped object lifetimes can end earlier. Heap allocations can outlive the allocating call; reclamation follows ownership, reachability or explicit deallocation rather than actual future need. The rest of this module is really about the heap, so it pays to understand why the stack is the easy case.

> [!note] Scope of this module
> The Operating Systems subject covers virtual memory, pages and how `malloc` carves up memory internally. Here we take the language-level view: who decides when a value dies, and how.

## The call stack

When a function is called, the program pushes a **stack frame** holding its parameters, local variables and the return address. When the function returns, the frame is popped and all of it disappears at once.

```
 main() calls area(), which calls sq()

 high addresses
 +----------------------+
 | main:  w=3, h=4      |
 +----------------------+
 | area:  a=3, b=4      |
 |        ret -> main   |
 +----------------------+
 | sq:    n=3           |  <- stack pointer
 |        ret -> area   |
 +----------------------+
 low addresses (grows down on x86/ARM)
```

Allocating a frame is just moving the **stack pointer** register by a fixed amount, usually a single instruction. Freeing it is moving the pointer back. The simple LIFO fast path needs no free-list search. Prologues, alignment, stack checks, page faults and runtime stack growth can add work; cache residency is not guaranteed.

The catch is that the stack is strictly **last in, first out**. A frame cannot outlive the call that created it, and the compiler usually needs to know each frame's size in advance.

## The heap

The **heap** is a large pool of memory where blocks can be allocated and freed in any order. Heap storage is commonly useful when:

1. A value must **outlive the function** that created it (returning a new object, storing it in a global or a long-lived data structure).
2. The **size is only known at run time** (reading a file of unknown length, a list that grows).
3. The value is **large** (a 50 MB image would blow the stack).
4. The value is **shared** between threads or parts of the program with unrelated lifetimes.

Heap allocation often costs more, although bump-pointer heap allocators also have cheap fast paths: the allocator must find a free block, record its size and later reclaim it. The really hard question is **when to free it**, because its lifetime need not coincide with the allocating call. That question is the subject of every other lesson in this module.

## The classic bug: returning a stack address

C distinguishes storage durations; it does not require a physical stack. Automatic locals commonly use frames or registers, static locals use static storage, and malloc obtains allocated storage.

```c
#include <stdlib.h>

int *bad(void) {
    int x = 42;
    return &x;   /* frame dies here */
}

int *good(void) {
    int *p = malloc(sizeof *p);
    if (!p) return NULL;
    *p = 42;
    return p;    /* caller must free */
}
```

`bad` returns the address of a slot in a frame that has already been popped. Accessing the expired object is undefined behavior regardless of whether later calls reuse that storage; no particular output or crash is guaranteed. Clang warns: *address of stack memory associated with local variable 'x' returned*. `good` returns NULL on allocation failure; on success the caller has a new duty: call `free(p)` exactly once.

## How each language places values

| Language | Stack | Heap |
|---|---|---|
| C | many automatic locals; placement optimized | allocated storage from malloc |
| CPython | implementation-specific interpreter frames | most objects; some shared/static objects |
| Java | local slots conceptually; may be registers | objects in JVM model; allocations may be eliminated |
| Go | non-escaping values | escaping values |
| Rust | local values often inline or registers | owned allocations through Box, Vec, String |

### Python: names reference managed objects

CPython represents values as objects with type and reference-management metadata. Most are dynamically allocated; some singleton/static objects and immortal objects are exceptions, and free-threaded builds have different counting details. A few, such as small integers and `None`, are created once when the interpreter starts and shared. A local variable is just a name in the frame that **refers** to an object.

```python
def make():
    xs = [1, 2, 3]   # list object on heap
    return xs        # return the reference

a = make()       # list survives the call
```

The list survives this call because `a` still refers to it. That is why "stack vs heap" rarely comes up in Python: you never place anything yourself, and the runtime manages reclamation; cycles and finalization complicate promptness (lesson 3).

### Java: primitives and references on the stack, objects on the heap

In Java, a local `int` lives in the frame, and so does a local reference variable, but the object it points to is always (semantically) on the heap.

```java
void f() {
    int n = 10;            // in frame
    int[] a = new int[n];  // ref in frame,
                           // array on heap
}
```

The HotSpot JIT compiler performs **escape analysis**: if it can prove an object never leaves the method, it may eliminate the allocation entirely and keep the fields in registers ("scalar replacement"). You cannot request this; it is an optimisation.

### Go: the compiler decides with escape analysis

Go makes escape analysis visible. You can return a pointer to a local variable, and it is perfectly safe:

```go
type Point struct{ X, Y int }

func newPoint() *Point {
    p := Point{1, 2}
    return &p   // fine in Go
}
```

Analyzed as a non-inlined function returning an escaping pointer, p requires storage surviving the call and the standard compiler normally heap-allocates it. Inlining can change the result at a particular call site. Use go build -gcflags=-m to inspect decisions; nonescaping values can still need heap storage for implementation reasons such as size.

Things that commonly force a value to escape in Go: returning its address, storing it in a global or a heap object, capturing it in a closure that outlives the call, or storing an interface value in an escaping location. Merely forming a pointer or interface does not universally force heap allocation.

### Rust: ownership and explicit allocations

Rust values can live in locals, registers, static storage or inside another allocation. Box owns a heap allocation, while Vec and String usually own buffers. A local Vec or String commonly has inline pointer/length/capacity metadata; a Box<T> for sized T has a pointer-sized representation, not those three fields, and the buffer is freed automatically when the owner goes out of scope (lesson 6).

```
 let v = vec![1, 2, 3];

 stack            heap
 +----------+     +---+---+---+
 | ptr  ----+---> | 1 | 2 | 3 |
 | len  = 3 |     +---+---+---+
 | cap  = 3 |
 +----------+
```

## Stack limits and stack overflow

Stacks are small compared with the heap, and each thread has its own.

| Runtime | Typical stack size |
|---|---|
| Linux main thread | configured limit; inspect ulimit -s |
| JVM platform thread | platform/version-dependent; configure -Xss |
| Go standard runtime goroutine | small growable stack; implementation-dependent |
| CPython | interpreter recursion limit; inspect sys.getrecursionlimit() |

Deep or unbounded recursion overflows the stack: a segmentation fault in C, `StackOverflowError` in Java, a fatal "goroutine stack exceeds" error in Go (the default maximum is 1 GB on 64-bit), and `RecursionError` in Python (which counts frames rather than bytes).

Goroutine stacks are a neat trick. They start tiny and, when a function needs more room, the runtime allocates a bigger stack and copies the old one across, fixing up pointers into it. That is why a Go program can run hundreds of thousands of goroutines when the same number of 1 MB OS-thread stacks would not fit.

> [!warning] Big arrays on the stack
> If double is 8 bytes and the array is materialized on the stack, `double grid[2000][2000];` needs 32,000,000 bytes, exceeding an 8 MiB stack budget. Allocate it on the heap instead.

> [!note] Limits of this model
> A universal stack size or allocation latency is omitted: neither is guaranteed across runtimes, operating systems and compiler settings. Dynamic size and sharing alone do not require heap storage (C VLAs and safely scoped sharing are counterexamples).

## Value and reference semantics

Placement is tied to what assignment means:

- **Value semantics**: assignment copies the data. C structs, Go structs and arrays, and Rust's `Copy` types behave this way.
- **Reference semantics**: assignment copies a pointer, so two names share one object. Python objects and Java objects behave this way.

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = a          # same list, not a copy
b.append(3)
print(a)       # [1, 2, 3]
```

Shared heap objects are exactly what makes deallocation hard: you can only free the list when **neither** `a` nor `b` can reach it.

## Trade-offs at a glance

| | Stack | Heap |
|---|---|---|
| Allocate | move a pointer | allocator call |
| Free | automatic, at return | manual or GC |
| Lifetime | the call | any |
| Size | fixed, small | flexible, large |

Performance-minded code in managed languages tries to **avoid heap allocation in hot loops**: reuse buffers, prefer values over pointers in Go, and let escape analysis keep short-lived objects off the heap. Every avoided allocation is also work the garbage collector never has to do.

## Key takeaways
- Conventional call frames use LIFO allocation; physical placement and object lifetimes depend on the language and implementation.
- The heap holds anything that outlives its creator, is sized at run time, is large or is shared; deciding when to free it is the hard problem.
- C exposes storage duration and allocated storage; managed runtimes choose representations and may eliminate allocations; Rust separates ownership from physical storage placement.
- Returning a pointer to a local is a bug in C but safe in Go, because Go's compiler moves the value to the heap.
- Stacks are small (megabytes per thread, kilobytes per goroutine), so deep recursion and large local arrays overflow them.

questions.prompt: Why can a conventional fixed-size stack-frame allocation have a cheap fast path?

options.text: The stack lives in faster RAM chips than the heap
options.explanation: Stack and heap are both ordinary virtual memory in the same RAM. The speed difference comes from the bookkeeping, not the hardware (although stack memory is usually hot in cache).

options.text: Allocating a frame is just moving the stack pointer by a fixed amount, and freeing it is moving it back
options.explanation: Correct. LIFO placement allows a stack-pointer adjustment rather than a free-list search. Prologues, checks, alignment, faults and growth can add work; heap bump allocation can also be cheap.

options.text: The operating system pre-zeroes stack memory, so no work is needed
options.explanation: Whether memory is zeroed has nothing to do with allocation cost; C locals are not even initialised. The saving is the absence of any allocator bookkeeping.

options.text: Stack values are never freed, so there is no deallocation cost
options.explanation: Stack values are freed, automatically and all at once, when the function returns. That is precisely why they cannot outlive the call.

questions.workedExample:
1. Think about what a heap allocator must do: find a free block big enough, record its size, and later accept it back in any order.
2. A stack frame is freed in the reverse order it was created, always.
3. With LIFO order, the free space is always one contiguous region above the stack pointer.
4. So allocation is `sp -= frame_size` and freeing is `sp += frame_size`.

The price of that speed is the LIFO restriction: nothing in the frame can outlive the call.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
```

options.explanation: This assumes `b = a` copies the list (value semantics). In Python, assignment copies only the reference, so both names point at one heap object.
Correct. There is one list object on the heap and two names referring to it. Appending through `b` changes the object that `a` also sees.
Only one `append` runs, on one object. Nothing appends twice.

options.text: An error, because `a` and `b` cannot share a list
options.explanation: Sharing objects through multiple references is normal in Python; it is what reference semantics means.

questions.workedExample:
1. `a = [1, 2]` creates a list object on the heap and binds the name `a` to it.
2. `b = a` binds `b` to the **same** object. No copy is made.

```
a --+
    +--> [1, 2]
b --+
```

3. `b.append(3)` mutates that object to `[1, 2, 3]`.
4. `print(a)` follows `a` to the same object: `[1, 2, 3]`.

To get an independent copy you would write `b = a.copy()` or `b = list(a)`.

questions.prompt: Which value most clearly calls for storage surviving the allocating call, commonly a heap allocation?

options.text: A loop counter `i` used inside one function
options.explanation: A counter whose lifetime is one call is the textbook stack value: fixed size and dies when the function returns.

options.text: A fixed-size `int point[2]` used only inside the function that declares it
options.explanation: Small, fixed-size and confined to one call: the stack handles this perfectly.

options.text: A list of lines read from a file of unknown length, returned to the caller
options.explanation: Correct. Its size is only known at run time and it must outlive the function that builds it. Both are reasons for the heap.

options.text: A function parameter `n` of type `int`
options.explanation: Parameters live in the callee's frame (or registers) and die with the call. No heap needed.

questions.workedExample:
Ask the four heap questions for each value:

| Value | Outlives call? | Size at run time? |
|---|---|---|
| loop counter | no | no |
| `point[2]` | no | no |
| file lines | **yes** | **yes** |
| parameter `n` | no | no |

Only the list of lines fails the stack's rules: it must survive the return, and the compiler cannot know how big a frame it would need.

This is a common design choice, not a proof that dynamic size or sharing always requires the heap. Caller-provided storage, static storage and other lifetime arrangements can be alternatives.

options.text: `x` is a global variable, so other threads overwrite it
options.explanation: `x` is a local (automatic) variable, not a global. The problem is its lifetime, not sharing between threads.

options.text: `printf` cannot print through a pointer
options.explanation: Dereferencing a valid `int *` with `*p` is fine. The pointer is the problem, not `printf`.

options.text: x has automatic storage duration ending at return; accessing it afterward is undefined behavior
options.explanation: Correct. Stack reuse is one possible manifestation, not a necessary condition or guaranteed explanation of observed output.

options.text: The compiler automatically moves `x` to the heap, but frees it before `printf`
options.explanation: That is what Go does (minus the early free). C never moves locals to the heap; it just warns that you returned a stack address.

questions.workedExample: The lifetime of x ends when get returns. Reading through the returned pointer is undefined behavior immediately; optimization or later frame reuse can produce arbitrary symptoms, and no particular value or crash is guaranteed. Return an int value, use caller-provided storage, or allocate and check heap storage with documented ownership.

options.text: It returns a dangling pointer, exactly like the C equivalent
options.explanation: That is C's behaviour. Go's compiler tracks pointers out of a function and never lets a stack slot be referenced after the frame dies.

options.text: It fails to compile: you cannot take the address of a local
options.explanation: Taking `&p` of a local is legal and idiomatic Go.

options.text: Escape analysis sees that `p` outlives the call and allocates it on the heap; the GC frees it later
options.explanation: Correct. `go build -gcflags=-m` reports `moved to heap: p`. The pointer is valid for as long as anyone holds it.

options.text: `p` is copied into the caller's stack frame on return
options.explanation: The return type is a pointer, not a Point copy. Inlining and caller context can sometimes eliminate heap allocation, but that is excluded by this question’s premise.

questions.workedExample:
1. The compiler runs escape analysis on `newPoint`.
2. It sees `&p` flowing out through the return value.
3. A stack slot cannot survive the return, so `p` is allocated on the heap instead.
4. The returned pointer refers to that heap object, and the garbage collector reclaims it once nothing references it.

If `newPoint` returned `Point` (a value) instead, `p` could stay on the stack and be copied out, costing the GC nothing.

Assume Point is declared as struct{ X,Y int }. The language guarantees the pointer remains valid, not a fixed placement decision at every optimized call site.

questions.prompt: Analyzing these Go functions without inlining into callers, with returned references retained, which locals escape? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Escapes. The address leaves the function through the return value, so `x` must outlive the frame.

options.text:
```go
func b() int {
    x := 1
    p := &x
    return *p
}
```
options.explanation: Does not escape. `p` is used only inside `b` and only the value `*p` is returned, so `x` can stay on the stack. Taking an address does not by itself force a heap allocation.

options.text:
```go
var g *int

func c() {
    x := 1
    g = &x
}
```
options.explanation: Escapes. Storing the address in a global means it is reachable after `c` returns.
Escapes. The returned closure captures `c` by reference and outlives `d`, so `c` must live on the heap.

questions.workedExample:
The rule: a value escapes if a reference to it can be reached after its function returns.

| Fn | Reference leaves? | Escapes |
|---|---|---|
| a | via return | yes |
| b | no, only a copy | no |
| c | via global | yes |
| d | via closure | yes |

You can confirm each with `go build -gcflags=-m`, which can report escaping x in a/c and captured c in d; diagnostic wording depends on the compiler. Optimized call-site behavior can differ.

questions.prompt: Assume a recursive C call consumes 128 bytes with no tail-call elimination, and its thread has an 8 MiB stack budget. Roughly how many frames fit, ignoring existing stack use?

options.text: About 6,500 calls
options.explanation: That is 8 MB divided by roughly 1,280 bytes, ten times the frame size given.

options.text: About 65,000 calls
options.explanation: Correct. 8 MiB is 8,388,608 bytes; divided by 128 bytes per frame that is 65,536 frames, minus a little for `main` and the C runtime.

options.text: About 8 million calls
options.explanation: That treats each call as using 1 byte. A frame holds the return address, saved registers and locals, so it is tens to hundreds of bytes.

options.text: Unlimited, because the stack grows into the heap as needed
options.explanation: A thread's stack has a fixed maximum (set by `ulimit -s` for the main thread). Exceed it and you hit a guard page and crash with a segmentation fault.

questions.workedExample: 8 MiB = 8 × 1,048,576 = 8,388,608 bytes. Dividing by 128 yields 65,536 frames. Real available depth is lower because of existing frames, guards and implementation overhead; actual frame and stack sizes must be measured.

options.text: count is a primitive local value in f’s frame model
options.explanation: True. Local primitives live in the frame (or registers) and vanish when `f` returns.

options.text: a is a reference local in f’s frame model
options.explanation: True. The local variable holds a reference (pointer-sized), and that reference lives in the frame.

options.text: The array object is allocated on the stack because `a` is a local
options.explanation: False. In Java's model every object, including arrays, is on the heap. Only the reference is local. (The JIT may optimise away a non-escaping allocation, but that is an optimisation, not the semantics.)

options.text: The array becomes eligible for garbage collection once `f` returns
options.explanation: True. After the return no reference to the array exists, so the next collection that examines it can reclaim it.

questions.workedExample:
Separate the variable from the object it refers to:

```
 frame of f        heap
 +-----------+     +--------------+
 | n         |     | int[n]       |
 | count     |     | 0 0 0 ...    |
 | a  -------+---> +--------------+
 +-----------+
```

1. `count` and `a` are locals, so both live in the frame.
2. `new` always creates the object on the heap.
3. When `f` returns, the frame and the only reference disappear, so the array is unreachable and collectable.

Optimized machine code may keep locals in registers or eliminate them and the array. The array may become unreachable before return after its last possible use.

questions.prompt: For a sizing model, assume 100,000 goroutines each start with a 2 KiB stack, versus 100,000 Java platform threads each reserving a configured 1 MiB stack. Roughly how much initial stack space is involved, ignoring all other overhead?

options.text: Go about 200 MB; Java about 100 GB reserved
options.explanation: Correct. 100,000 × ~2 KB ≈ 200 MB for goroutines; 100,000 × 1 MB ≈ 100 GB of reserved stack for threads. The OS commits thread stack pages lazily, but the reservations, kernel thread structures and scheduling cost still make this impractical.

options.text: Both about 100 GB, because stacks are the same everywhere
options.explanation: Goroutine stacks are managed by the Go runtime, not the OS. They start at a few kilobytes and grow by copying, so they are far smaller than OS thread stacks.

options.text: Go about 200 KB; Java about 100 MB
options.explanation: Off by a factor of 1,000 in both cases: 100,000 × 2 KB is 200,000 KB, about 200 MB.

options.text: Go 0, because goroutines have no stack
options.explanation: Every goroutine has its own stack; it is just small and growable.

questions.workedExample: Goroutine stack bytes: 100,000 × 2,048 = 204,800,000 B, about 205 MB. Platform-thread reservations: 100,000 × 1,048,576 = 104,857,600,000 B, about 105 GB. The rounded answer is about 200 MB versus 100 GB. These are assumed sizes, not universal defaults or predictions of resident memory.

questions.prompt: A Java developer says: "My `Point` objects are created and discarded inside one hot loop, so the JVM puts them on the stack." What is the most accurate response?

options.text: Correct: the JVM always stack-allocates objects that are created inside a loop
options.explanation: The JVM makes no such guarantee. Placement depends on the JIT's analysis of each allocation site after inlining.

options.text: Wrong: Java objects are always heap-allocated and every one costs a GC allocation
options.explanation: Too strong. Semantically objects are on the heap, but HotSpot's C2 compiler can eliminate allocations it proves never escape.

options.text: Partly right: if the JIT's escape analysis proves the object never escapes, it can scalar-replace it, keeping its fields in registers or the frame with no heap allocation
options.explanation: Correct. HotSpot C2 can scalar-replace eligible allocations. Escape and scalar-replacement eligibility depend on compiler analysis; nonescaping alone is not a guarantee.

options.text: Wrong: escape analysis is only done by Go, never by the JVM
options.explanation: HotSpot has done escape analysis since Java 6 (`-XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis`, on by default). Go simply makes its version visible with `-gcflags=-m`.

questions.workedExample: The JVM object model does not promise stack allocation. HotSpot C2 can eliminate some allocations by scalar replacement, making their fields locals or registers. Non-inlined calls or storage into escaping objects can obstruct analysis, but using a nonescaping object as a lock need not: escape analysis can also eliminate locking. Measure the optimized allocation behavior.

questions.prompt: For a materialized local Vec<i32> on a conventional target with 8-byte pointers and usize, use the standard pointer/length/capacity model. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The Vec value has pointer, length and capacity metadata: 24 bytes in this model
options.explanation: The default-allocator Vec guarantees this triplet; field order is not promised and optimized locals need not occupy physical stack slots.

options.text: The three `i32` elements (12 bytes) live in a heap buffer owned by `v`
options.explanation: True. `vec!` allocates a heap buffer and the `Vec` owns it.

options.text: The heap buffer is freed when the garbage collector next runs
options.explanation: False. Rust has no garbage collector. The buffer is freed deterministically when `v` goes out of scope (its `Drop` runs).

options.text: `let w = v;` copies the 24-byte header, not the heap buffer, and `v` can no longer be used
options.explanation: True. This is a move: the pointer, length and capacity are copied into `w`, ownership transfers, and the compiler rejects later uses of `v` so the buffer is never freed twice.

questions.workedExample:
Draw the layout:

```
 stack (v)        heap
 +-----------+    +---+---+---+
 | ptr  -----+--> | 1 | 2 | 3 |
 | len = 3   |    +---+---+---+
 | cap = 3   |     12 bytes
 +-----------+
  3 x 8 = 24 bytes
```

1. Three words on the stack: 24 bytes.
2. Three 4-byte integers on the heap: 12 bytes.
3. Freeing happens when the owner's scope ends, with no GC.
4. `let w = v;` copies the three words and marks `v` as moved. Only `w` will free the buffer.

This describes the ownership/layout model; the compiler can eliminate physical copies or allocations when observable behavior is preserved.

lessons.title: Manual memory and its bugs
lessons.summary: The malloc/free contract seen from the programmer's side, the five classic bugs it invites, why they become security holes, and the tools and disciplines (ownership rules, RAII, arenas, sanitizers) that tame them.

options.text: Nothing; `strlen` counts every byte the string needs
options.explanation: `strlen` counts the characters but not the terminating NUL byte, so the buffer is one byte short.

options.text: It leaks memory because it never calls `free`
options.explanation: Returning the pointer hands ownership to the caller, which is the normal pattern. Not freeing inside `copy` is correct; the caller must free it.

options.text: It writes one byte past the end of the block
options.explanation: Correct. `strcpy` copies the characters plus the NUL terminator, which is `strlen(src) + 1` bytes, into a block of `strlen(src)` bytes: a one-byte heap overflow.

options.text: It returns the address of a stack variable
options.explanation: `s` itself is a local, but it holds a heap address from `malloc`. Returning the value of a pointer to heap memory is fine.

questions.workedExample:
1. `src = "hi"` has `strlen` 2, but occupies 3 bytes: `h`, `i`, `\0`.
2. `malloc(2)` returns a 2-byte block.
3. `strcpy` writes 3 bytes, so the NUL lands one byte past the end.

```
block:  [ h ][ i ] | \0  <- overflow
```

4. The fix is `malloc(strlen(src) + 1)`, or simply `strdup(src)`.

Off-by-one overflows like this often corrupt the allocator's metadata for the next block and crash much later, far from the bug.

A real repair must also check allocation failure before strcpy. These statements describe an unsafe demonstration, not a safe complete copy routine.

questions.prompt: A pointer still holds the address of a block that has been passed to `free`. What is that pointer called, and what is using it?

options.text: A dangling pointer; using it is a use-after-free
options.explanation: Correct. The pointer refers to memory the program no longer owns. Reading or writing through it is undefined behaviour and a common exploit primitive.

options.text: A null pointer; using it is a null dereference
options.explanation: `free` does not change the pointer's value. It still holds the old, non-null address, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.

options.text: A wild pointer; using it is a memory leak
options.explanation: A leak is memory still allocated with no pointer to it, the opposite situation. Here the pointer survives but the memory has gone.

options.text: A smart pointer; using it is safe because the allocator tracks it
options.explanation: C's allocator does not track your pointers at all. Nothing stops you using a freed address.

questions.workedExample: After free, the allocation lifetime ends and aliases to it are dangling; reading or writing through them is undefined behavior. The stored bits are not automatically replaced with NULL, but the C pointer value becomes indeterminate under lifetime rules. Assigning p = NULL can prevent a second free through that variable because free(NULL) is allowed; dereferencing NULL remains undefined behavior and is not a guaranteed clean crash. Other aliases remain dangling.

questions.prompt: A small command-line tool runs for 200 ms, allocates a few megabytes and never calls `free`. A long-running server leaks 4,000 bytes on every request at 1,000 requests a second. Which statement is right?

options.text: Both are equally serious because every leak eventually crashes
options.explanation: A small bounded leak in a short-lived process differs from unbounded growth. It is not necessarily equally consequential.

options.text: Neither matters, because the OS frees leaked memory periodically
options.explanation: The OS only reclaims a process's memory when the process exits. It cannot know which blocks a running program still intends to use.

options.text: The server is fine because 4 KB is less than a page
options.explanation: Small leaks add up. Size per leak matters far less than the rate multiplied by uptime.

options.text: The short-lived allocation has limited retention cost; the server accumulates about 346 GB/day
options.explanation: Correct under the stated rate. Memory exhaustion risk grows, but failure timing and behavior depend on limits and allocation patterns.

questions.workedExample: In the assumed hosted process, exit reclaims the address space, so the small short-lived allocation has limited retention cost. The server accumulates 4,000 × 1,000 × 86,400 = 345,600,000,000 bytes/day, or 345.6 decimal GB. Time and type of resource failure depend on limits and workload; there is no guaranteed OOM-kill schedule.

options.text: It always prints `ann`, because `free` does not erase memory
options.explanation: It might print `ann`, but nothing guarantees it. The freed slot may already have been reused by the next allocation.

options.text: The second `malloc` fails because the memory is still referenced by `u`
options.explanation: The allocator has no idea `u` still exists. Once freed, the block is fair game for any allocation.

options.text: It is undefined behaviour; with typical allocators `m` may reuse `u`'s slot, so `u->name` reads bytes that now belong to `m`
options.explanation: Correct. This is a use-after-free. Many allocators hand a just-freed block of the same size straight back, so `u` and `m` alias, and `u->name` is now whatever bytes `m` put there.

options.text: It prints an empty string because `free` zeroes the block
options.explanation: Standard `free` does not zero memory. Some debugging allocators poison freed memory, but that is not the C contract.

questions.workedExample:
1. `free(u)` returns the block to the allocator. `u` still holds its address.
2. Allocators keep per-size free lists. A request for the same size often gets the most recently freed block back.
3. So `m` may equal `u`. Writing `m->text` overwrites the bytes where `u->name` used to be.
4. `u->name` is now interpreted from those bytes: garbage, a crash, or attacker-chosen data.

This is the core of many real exploits: free an object, get attacker-controlled data allocated into the same slot, then use the dangling pointer. AddressSanitizer reports it as `heap-use-after-free`.

questions.prompt: Which patterns can retain memory indefinitely after it is no longer useful in Java, Python or Go? Select all that apply. For the local-list case assume no references escape by any path.

options.text: A module-level dict used as a cache that is never evicted
options.explanation: Correct. Every entry stays reachable from a global, so the GC can never free it, even if it will never be read again.

options.text: An event listener registered on a long-lived object and never removed
options.explanation: Correct. The long-lived object holds a reference to the listener, and through it everything the listener captures.

options.text: A goroutine blocked forever receiving on a channel nobody sends to
options.explanation: Correct. A blocked goroutine is never collected, and its stack keeps everything it references alive.

options.text: A local list created inside a function and not returned
options.explanation: Once the function returns, nothing refers to the list, so it becomes unreachable and the GC reclaims it. That is the normal case GC handles.

options.text: Two objects that refer only to each other, in Java
options.explanation: Java's tracing collector frees anything unreachable from the roots, cycles included. (CPython's reference counting alone could not, but its cycle collector does.)

questions.workedExample:
A GC frees memory that is **unreachable**. A leak in a GC language is memory that is still **reachable** but will never be used.

1. Global cache: reachable from a module global. Leak.
2. Listener: reachable from the long-lived subject's listener list. Leak.
3. Blocked goroutine: goroutines are roots; its stack keeps its data alive. Leak.
4. Local list: no references after return. Collected.
5. Cycle in Java: unreachable from roots, so a tracing GC collects it.

The fix is the same in each leaky case: bound the structure (an LRU cache), unregister, or give the goroutine a way to exit (a `context` or a closed channel).

options.text: Because `goto` automatically frees memory allocated before it
options.explanation: `goto` is just a jump. It frees nothing by itself.

options.text: Because `buf` starts as `NULL`, every path reaches `out:`, and `free(NULL)` is defined to do nothing
options.explanation: Correct. Initialising to `NULL` means the early `goto` on a failed `fopen` reaches `free(buf)` with `buf == NULL`, which the C standard defines as a no-op.

options.text: Because the compiler inserts `free` calls at every `return`
options.explanation: C compilers never insert `free` calls. That is what RAII does in C++, not C.

options.text: It doesn't: when `fopen` fails, `free(buf)` is undefined behaviour
options.explanation: It would be if `buf` were uninitialised. Because it is set to `NULL` first, `free(NULL)` is well defined and harmless.

questions.workedExample:
Trace each path:

1. `fopen` fails: `buf` is `NULL`, jump to `out`. `free(NULL)` does nothing; `fp` is `NULL`, so no `fclose`. Return -1.
2. `malloc` fails: `fp` is open, `buf` is `NULL`. `free(NULL)` is a no-op; `fclose(fp)` runs. Return -1.
3. Success: both acquired, both released. Return 0.

Every path runs one cleanup block, so nothing leaks and nothing is freed twice. This single-exit pattern is used throughout the Linux kernel.

questions.prompt: A C++ function creates `auto p = std::make_unique<Widget>();` and then calls a function that throws an exception. What happens to the `Widget`? Assume a handler outside the function catches the exception, with normal stack unwinding.

options.text: It is freed when the exception unwinds the stack, because `p`'s destructor runs
options.explanation: Correct. Stack unwinding runs the destructors of every local object in the abandoned frames. `~unique_ptr` deletes the `Widget`. This is RAII.

options.text: It leaks, because the `delete` line after the call is skipped
options.explanation: That is what happens with a raw `new` and a manual `delete`. `unique_ptr` exists precisely to avoid it.

options.text: It is freed later by the C++ garbage collector
options.explanation: Standard C++ has no garbage collector. Memory is released deterministically by destructors.

options.text: The program terminates immediately, so it doesn't matter
options.explanation: An exception that is caught higher up does not terminate the program, and the destructors run during unwinding.

questions.workedExample:
1. RAII ties a resource to an object's lifetime.
2. `p` is a local object; its destructor runs whenever its scope ends, by normal return **or** by an exception.
3. During unwinding, C++ calls `~unique_ptr()`, which calls `delete` on the `Widget`.

Compare the raw version:

```cpp
Widget *w = new Widget;
mayThrow();     // throws
delete w;       // never reached: leak
```

The same idea frees locks (`std::lock_guard`), files and sockets.

questions.prompt: A compiler allocates millions of small AST nodes during one compilation pass and frees them all at the end. Which strategy is most appropriate, and why?

options.text: `malloc` and `free` each node individually, so memory is returned as early as possible
options.explanation: This works but pays the allocator cost millions of times and invites use-after-free and double-free bugs as nodes are shared across the tree.

options.text: An arena: bump-allocate nodes from large blocks and free the whole arena when the pass ends
options.explanation: Correct. Allocation is a pointer bump, there are no individual frees to get wrong, and the whole region goes in one call. This fits objects that share one lifetime.

options.text: Reference count each node so they free themselves
options.explanation: Reference counting adds a count update on every pointer copy and cannot free cycles (such as parent pointers) without help. It is overkill when every node dies at the same moment.

options.text: Put the nodes on the stack, since the pass is a single function call
options.explanation: Millions of nodes would overflow a stack of a few megabytes, and the pass is many nested calls, not one frame.

questions.workedExample:
1. Note the lifetime pattern: every node is born during the pass and dies at its end.
2. When objects share a lifetime, tracking them individually is wasted effort.
3. An arena grabs big chunks and hands out memory by bumping a pointer:

```
[node|node|node|node|  free...  ]
                    ^ next
```

4. At the end, free the chunks. No per-node bookkeeping, no dangling pointers within the pass.

Clang, Rust's compiler, game engines (per-frame arenas) and nginx (per-request pools) all use this.

questions.prompt: Your team runs its C test suite under AddressSanitizer and it reports no errors. Which conclusions are justified? Select all that apply.

options.text: The code paths the tests executed had no detected overflows or use-after-free bugs
options.explanation: Correct. ASan checks the accesses that actually happen while it runs.

options.text: The program is now free of memory-safety bugs
options.explanation: Sanitizers are dynamic: they only see the paths you exercise. Bugs in untested branches or on unusual inputs remain.

options.text: Fuzzing the parser under ASan is a sensible next step
options.explanation: Correct. Fuzzers generate the odd inputs that reach untested paths, and ASan turns silent corruption into a crash with a stack trace.

options.text: Running under ASan in production is free, so you should leave it on
options.explanation: ASan typically roughly doubles run time and uses noticeably more memory. Most teams use it in testing and fuzzing, not production.

options.text: Sound memory-safe abstractions can prevent these bug classes through static and/or runtime enforcement
options.explanation: Correct, subject to their safe-subset and implementation assumptions. Java/Go bounds checks and Rust static borrows are different mechanisms; not all prevention is static.

questions.workedExample:
1. ASan instruments loads and stores and keeps redzones around allocations. It reports errors **only when they happen** during a run.
2. A clean run says: no errors on these inputs and paths.
3. To widen coverage, combine it with fuzzers (libFuzzer, AFL), which is how many memory-safety bugs in large C/C++ projects are found.
4. Cost: about 2x slowdown plus extra memory, so it is a testing tool.
5. Absence of evidence is not proof; that gap is what memory-safe languages close.

questions.prompt: An attacker can make a server free an object containing a function pointer while a dangling pointer to it survives, and can then send a packet whose payload is copied into a newly allocated buffer of the same size. Why is this so dangerous?

options.text: It only causes a crash, because freed memory is unmapped from the process
options.explanation: Small freed blocks stay mapped and are recycled by the allocator. They are not unmapped, so they can be reused with new contents.

options.text: It leaks the old object's memory, eventually exhausting the heap
options.explanation: The memory is reused, not leaked. The problem is aliasing, not growth.

options.text: It is harmless if the server uses `calloc`, which zeroes memory
options.explanation: `calloc` zeroes the new block at allocation, but the attacker then fills it with their payload. Zeroing does not stop the aliasing.

options.text: The new buffer can occupy the freed slot, so the next call through the dangling pointer jumps to an address the attacker chose
options.explanation: Correct. This is the classic use-after-free exploitation pattern: reclaim the slot with controlled bytes, then let the program use its stale pointer to call or write somewhere useful to the attacker.

questions.workedExample: If the allocator reuses the freed slot, attacker-controlled bytes can replace a stored callback address. A later call through the dangling pointer can then redirect control flow unless mitigations stop it. Neither slot reuse nor successful code execution is guaranteed by C. Chromium’s cited historical analysis covered 912 high/critical bugs since 2015: about 70% involved memory unsafety, and about half of those were use-after-free.

questions.prompt: You must choose a tool to find a suspected use-after-free in a third-party Linux binary for which you have no source code. Which is the better first choice?

options.text: Valgrind Memcheck, because it runs unmodified binaries on a simulated CPU
options.explanation: Correct. Memcheck intercepts `malloc` and `free` and checks every access at run time without recompiling. The price is speed: roughly 20 to 30 times slower.

options.text: AddressSanitizer, because it is faster
options.explanation: ASan works by compile-time instrumentation, so it needs the source (or at least a rebuild). It cannot check an existing binary.

options.text: LeakSanitizer, because use-after-free is a kind of leak
options.explanation: Use-after-free is the opposite of a leak: the memory was freed too early, not never freed. LeakSanitizer also needs a sanitizer build.

options.text: Neither; use-after-free can only be found by code review
options.explanation: Dynamic tools find these routinely, with stack traces of the allocation, the free and the bad access.

1. Constraint: no source, so you cannot recompile with `-fsanitize=address`.
2. Valgrind translates the binary's machine code as it runs, adding checks to each memory access.
3. Trade-off table:

| | ASan | Memcheck |
|---|---|---|
| Rebuild | yes | no |
| Slowdown | ~2x | ~20-30x |

lessons.title: Reference counting and cycles
lessons.summary: Freeing an object the moment its last reference disappears, how CPython, Swift, C++ and Rust do it, what it costs, why cycles defeat it, and the weak references and cycle collectors that fix them.
lessons.body:
The simplest automatic answer to "when can this object be freed?" is: **when nobody refers to it any more**. Keep a counter in every object of how many references point at it. When the counter drops to zero, free the object.

That is **reference counting**. It runs inside CPython, Swift and Objective-C (as ARC), PHP, Perl, C++'s `std::shared_ptr` and Rust's `Rc` and `Arc`. It is easy to understand, it frees memory promptly, and it has one famous blind spot: **cycles**.

## The mechanism

In the basic model each managed allocation has a strong-reference count (possibly in a separate control block). The runtime (or the compiler) adjusts it whenever a reference is created or destroyed:

- A reference is **created** (assignment, passing an argument, putting it in a list): increment.
- A reference is **destroyed** (a variable is reassigned or goes out of scope, an item is removed): decrement.
- The count reaches **zero**: free the object, and decrement everything **it** refers to.

```
 a = Obj()        Obj  rc=1  <- a
 b = a            Obj  rc=2  <- a, b
 del a            Obj  rc=1  <- b
 b = None         Obj  rc=0  -> freed
```

That last rule makes freeing **recursive**. When the head of a linked list dies, its count of zero decrements the second node to zero, and so on down the list.

## Watching it in CPython

In ordinary GIL-enabled CPython, object headers include reference-count metadata. This simple non-resurrecting example illustrates prompt finalization; free-threaded/deferred counting, cycles and finalizers can alter timing:

```python
class Noisy:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def __del__(self):
        print("freed", self.name)

a = Noisy("a")
b = a
del a
print("after del a")
del b
print("after del b")
```

Output:

```
after del a
freed a
after del b
```

`del a` only drops the count from 2 to 1, because `b` still refers to the object. `del b` drops it to 0, so the object is freed immediately, before the next line runs.

> [!note] Immortal objects
> Since Python 3.12, objects such as `None`, `True` and small integers are **immortal** (PEP 683): reference-count operations treat them specially and ordinary decrements do not deallocate them. The large reported count is not a reliable count of live references or a stable universal constant.

## Why people like it

1. **Promptness.** Acyclic, non-resurrecting objects can be reclaimed promptly when their last strong owner releases them; allocator retention can still keep process memory high.
2. **Deterministic destruction.** Simple eager counting has predictable release points. For files use with/open, RAII or explicit close; temporary-object destruction is not a portable resource-management guarantee, and cycles or deferred counting can delay it.
3. **Incremental by nature.** The work is spread across the program, with no separate collector to pause everything (mostly; see below).
4. **Locality.** It only touches the objects being changed, not the whole heap.

## What it costs

Reference counting is not free. Creating or releasing a strong ownership reference can require count traffic. Borrowed references, moves, immortal objects and optimization can avoid updates.

- **Count updates everywhere.** Passing, storing or returning strong references can touch counts, depending on borrowing conventions and optimization. In CPython this is a measurable share of interpreter time.
- **Atomic operations under threads.** Concurrent strong-count updates require synchronization, often atomic operations whose cost depends on hardware, contention and memory ordering. C++ `shared_ptr` and Rust `Arc` pay this; Rust's `Rc` does not, and the compiler refuses to let an `Rc` cross threads. CPython's GIL let it use plain increments; the free-threaded build (PEP 703) uses **biased reference counting**, where the owning thread updates a fast local count and other threads use an atomic shared one.
- **Space.** Counts and related metadata use storage; their size varies by implementation (in `shared_ptr`, usually a separate control block).
- **Cascading frees.** Dropping the last reference to a 10-million-node tree frees 10 million objects right then. That is a pause, just one you caused yourself.
- **Copy-on-write damage.** Some operations acquiring references write counts, which can dirty shared pages after fork. The cycle collector also changes bookkeeping. gc.freeze() (Python 3.7) avoids collector traversal of frozen objects; it does not suppress their ordinary reference-count updates.

> [!tip] Avoiding count traffic
> C++ code passes `const std::shared_ptr<T>&`, or a plain `T&`, when the callee does not need to keep the object. Swift's optimiser removes retain/release pairs it can prove redundant. Rust makes clones of `Rc` explicit with `Rc::clone(&x)` so you can see each one.

## The cycle problem

Two objects that refer to each other each hold a count of at least 1, forever, even when nothing else can reach them.

```
 before:  x --> [A rc=2] --> [B rc=2] <-- y
                   ^------------'

 after del x, y:
          [A rc=1] --> [B rc=1]
             ^------------'
          unreachable, never freed
```

Cycles are everywhere in real programs: a parent node and its children with `parent` pointers, a doubly linked list, an object that registers itself as a callback, an exception that holds a traceback that holds the frame that holds the exception.

Pure counting cannot reclaim an unreachable strong-reference cycle that remains intact. Weak edges, explicit link removal or a design that forbids strong cycles can avoid that situation. There are two fixes: make some references not count (weak references), or add a separate collector that finds cycles.

## Fix 1: weak references

A **weak reference** points at an object without contributing to its count. When the object is freed, the weak reference becomes empty instead of dangling.

The rule of thumb: **owners hold strong references, back-pointers are weak.** A parent owns its children; a child's pointer to its parent is weak.

| Language | Strong | Weak |
|---|---|---|
| Python | normal ref | `weakref.ref` |
| Swift | default strong | weak (nil on release); unowned has a different lifetime contract |
| C++ | `shared_ptr` | `weak_ptr` |
| Rust | `Rc` / `Arc` | `Weak` |

```python
import weakref

class Node:
    def __init__(self, parent=None):
        self.children = []
        self._parent = (weakref.ref(parent)
                        if parent else None)

    @property
    def parent(self):
        ref = self._parent
        return ref() if ref else None
```

Calling the weak reference returns the object, or `None` if it has been freed. C++'s `weak_ptr::lock()` and Rust's `Weak::upgrade()` work the same way: they give you a temporary strong reference or nothing.

Swift adds `unowned`, a reference that does not keep its target strongly alive. You promise its target remains alive whenever it is accessed. Ordinary checked `unowned` traps on access after deallocation; `unowned(unsafe)` omits that protection. Swift closures are the classic cycle: a view controller stores a closure that captures `self` strongly. The fix is a capture list, `{ [weak self] in ... }`.

Weak references only help where you can see the cycle coming. Ordinary Swift/Objective-C ARC and C++ `shared_ptr` have no general tracing cycle collector. Explicitly clearing links can also break a cycle; a retained cycle otherwise leaks. Xcode provides a memory graph debugger to investigate such ownership.

## Fix 2: a cycle collector

CPython takes the belt-and-braces route: reference counting for the common case, plus a **cycle collector** in the `gc` module for the rest.

It only needs to consider **container** objects (lists, dicts, class instances), because ordinary built-in int and str instances do not contain references participating in cycles; subclasses and extension types can have different layouts. The algorithm is neat:

1. For each container being examined, copy its reference count into a scratch field.
2. For every reference *between* those containers, subtract one from the target's scratch count.
3. Anything left with a scratch count above zero is referenced from **outside** the group, so it is alive. Everything reachable from it is alive too.
4. Whatever remains is referenced only from inside the group: unreachable cycles. Free it.

```python
import gc
gc.disable()  # explicit collect still works

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.other = name, None
    def __del__(self):
        print("freed", self.name)

x, y = Node("x"), Node("y")
x.other, y.other = y, x
del x, y
print("after del")
gc.collect()
print("collected")
gc.enable()
```

Output (the two "freed" lines may come in either order):

```
after del
freed x
freed y
collected
```

After `del x, y`, each node still has a count of 1 from the other, so nothing is freed. `gc.collect()` subtracts the internal references, finds both at zero, and frees them. Since Python 3.4 (PEP 442), objects with `__del__` in a cycle are collected normally. Before that, they were parked uncollectable in `gc.garbage`.

The collector is **generational**: new containers are examined often, survivors less often, because most objects die young (lesson 4). Scheduling depends on version/build: net allocation counts matter, and free-threaded CPython also considers process-memory growth. The thresholds are tunable with `gc.set_threshold()`.

> [!warning] Disabling the cycle collector
> gc.disable() disables automatic cyclic collection. Reference counting still operates and explicit gc.collect() still works; unreachable intact strong cycles can accumulate until explicitly collected or broken. Some services do this deliberately for predictable latency and then must avoid creating cycles.

## Where reference counting sits

| | Ref counting | Tracing GC |
|---|---|---|
| When freed | last strong release in the basic acyclic model | during collection |
| Cycles | need extra help | free |
| Cost paid on | strong-reference updates and cascading release | collection and barriers |
| Destructors | deterministic | not timed |

Many systems blend the two. CPython is reference counting plus a tracing cycle collector. Research collectors use **deferred** reference counting, which skips count updates for stack variables and reconciles them periodically, to get most of the promptness with much less overhead.

## Key takeaways
- Reference counting frees an object the moment its count reaches zero, and frees its children recursively.
- Eager counting often gives prompt destruction, but cycles, resurrection and deferred counting are exceptions; use explicit resource-management constructs for files and locks.
- The costs include strong-reference count traffic, synchronization for shared counts and possible long cascading releases; optimized or borrowed references can avoid updates.
- Cycles are never freed by counting alone. Fix them with weak back-pointers (`weakref`, `weak`, `weak_ptr`, `Weak`) or a cycle collector.
- CPython combines counting with a generational cycle collector that finds groups referenced only from inside themselves.

## Further reading
- [Reference counting — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_counting)
- [Python gc module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/gc.html)
- [Python weakref module documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/weakref.html)
- [Automatic Reference Counting — The Swift Programming Language](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/automaticreferencecounting/)
- [Rc and reference cycles — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-06-reference-cycles.html)
- [PEP 683: Immortal objects](https://peps.python.org/pep-0683/)
- [Primary verification source 2](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/refcounting.html)
- [Primary verification source 3](https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/)
- [Primary verification source 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift-book/main/TSPL.docc/LanguageGuide/AutomaticReferenceCounting.md)

options.explanation: Setting `a = None` drops the count from 2 to 1, not to 0, because `b` still refers to the object. Nothing is freed yet.

options.explanation: Correct. The object is freed the instant its count hits zero, which is when `b = None` runs, just before `print("two")`.

options.text: `one`, `two`, `freed`
options.explanation: That would be the behaviour of a tracing GC that runs later, or at exit. CPython's reference counting frees immediately.

options.text: `one`, `two` and never `freed`
options.explanation: There is no cycle here, so reference counting alone frees the object as soon as the last reference goes.

questions.workedExample:
Track the count:

| Line | rc |
|---|---|
| `a = N()` | 1 |
| `b = a` | 2 |
| `a = None` | 1 |
| `b = None` | 0, freed |

1. `print("one")` runs while rc is 1.
2. `b = None` takes it to 0; `__del__` prints `freed` straight away.
3. Then `print("two")`.

This promptness is a defining property of reference counting.

questions.prompt: Why can't pure reference counting free two objects that refer only to each other?

options.text: Because their counts are both at least 1, held by each other, so neither ever reaches zero
options.explanation: Correct. Each object's count includes the reference from the other. Without outside help, neither count can drop to zero.

options.text: Because reference counts can't go below 1
options.explanation: Counts reach zero all the time; that is when objects are freed. The problem is specifically the references inside the cycle.

options.text: Because the objects are on the stack
options.explanation: Reference-counted objects live on the heap. Placement is not the issue.

options.text: Because the counter overflows
options.explanation: A two-object cycle has small counts. Overflow has nothing to do with it.

questions.workedExample:
1. `A.other = B` gives B rc ≥ 1; `B.other = A` gives A rc ≥ 1.
2. Drop all outside references: each count falls by those, but the internal ones remain.

```
[A rc=1] --> [B rc=1]
   ^------------'
```

3. Counting asks "does anything point at me?", not "can the program reach me?". For a cycle those questions have different answers.

A tracing collector asks the second question, which is why it handles cycles naturally.

questions.prompt: A tree node holds a list of its children and a pointer to its parent. Which reference should be weak to avoid a reference cycle? Assume parents own their children and children may observe a missing parent.

options.text: The parent's references to its children
options.explanation: If the children list were weak, children would be freed as soon as you stopped holding them elsewhere: the tree would fall apart. Parents own their children.

options.text: Both
options.explanation: If both were weak, nothing would keep the children alive once you let go of them.

options.text: Neither: reference counting handles trees fine
options.explanation: A parent pointer plus a child list is a cycle (parent → child → parent), which pure counting leaks.

options.text: The child's pointer to its parent
options.explanation: Correct. Owners hold strong references; back-pointers are weak. When the root is dropped, the strong chain down the tree frees everything.

questions.workedExample:
1. Draw the references:

```
parent --strong--> child
child  --?------> parent
```

2. If both are strong, that is a cycle of length 2.
3. Ownership flows downward, so make the upward pointer weak.
4. Dropping the root: root rc → 0, freed; it decrements each child to 0; they free their children, and so on.

Python `weakref.ref`, Swift `weak`, C++ `weak_ptr` and Rust `Weak` all express this.

Dropping the root only destroys children that have no other strong owners. A child retained elsewhere can survive with an empty weak parent reference.

class N:
    def __del__(self):

a, b = N(), N()
a.o, b.o = b, a

print("Y")

options.text: `freed`, `freed`, `X`, `Y`
options.explanation: `del` only removes the names. Each object still holds the other, so neither count reaches zero at that point.

options.text: `X`, `Y`, and the objects leak forever
options.explanation: Pure reference counting alone cannot collect the cycle, but gc.collect() explicitly invokes CPython’s collector even if automatic collection was disabled.

1. After `del a, b`: each object rc = 1 (held by the other). Nothing freed.
2. `print("X")`.
3. `gc.collect()`:
   - copy rc into scratch: A=1, B=1
   - subtract internal refs: A=0, B=0

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine costs of reference counting compared with a tracing collector? Select all that apply.

options.text: Strong-reference creation/release can add memory writes throughout otherwise read-only code
options.explanation: Correct. Borrowed references, moves, immortal objects and optimizations can avoid some updates.

options.text: Atomic increments and decrements when objects are shared between threads
options.explanation: Correct for thread-safe counting designs such as Arc/shared_ptr; synchronization cost depends on contention and hardware.

options.text: It cannot free any object until the whole heap is scanned
options.explanation: That describes a tracing collector's cycle. Reference counting frees each object as soon as its count hits zero.

options.text: Dropping the last reference to a huge structure frees all of it at once, causing a pause
options.explanation: Correct. Freeing is recursive, so releasing a 10-million-node tree does 10 million frees right there.

options.text: It needs twice the heap, like a copying collector
options.explanation: Reference counting adds a count per object, not a second semispace.

questions.workedExample: Counting adds traffic for strong ownership-reference creation and release, may need atomic synchronization across threads, and can trigger expensive release cascades. Borrowed references and optimizations can avoid updates. It does not intrinsically require a whole-heap scan or a spare semispace.

questions.prompt: A Swift view controller stores a closure in a property: `self.onTap = { self.count += 1 }`. The controller is dismissed but never deinitialised. Why, and what is the usual fix?

options.text: The controller holds the closure strongly and the closure captures `self` strongly: a cycle. Capture `[weak self]`.
options.explanation: Correct. Swift's ARC has no cycle collector, so this cycle leaks. `{ [weak self] in self?.count += 1 }` breaks it.

options.text: ARC doesn't track closures, so they're never freed; mark the property `static`
options.explanation: ARC does count closures; a closure that captures `self` holds a strong reference to it. `static` would make it worse by making it global.

options.text: ARC frees objects only when memory runs low; wait for a memory warning
options.explanation: ARC frees deterministically when the count hits zero, not under memory pressure.

options.text: Closures are on the stack; move it to the heap with `Box`
options.explanation: That is Rust vocabulary. Escaping closures in Swift are heap objects already; the issue is the strong capture.

questions.workedExample:
1. `self.onTap` → closure: strong.
2. Closure captures `self`: strong.

```
VC --strong--> closure
 ^---strong------'
```

3. When the navigation stack lets go of the VC, both counts are still 1. ARC has no tracing backup, so it leaks.
4. Fix with a capture list:

```swift
self.onTap = { [weak self] in
    self?.count += 1
}
```

Inside, `self` is optional and becomes `nil` once the VC is freed.

questions.prompt: A team runs a Python service with `gc.disable()` to remove collection pauses. What happens to memory?

options.text: Nothing is ever freed, so memory grows without bound
options.explanation: `gc.disable()` only switches off the cycle collector. Reference counting still frees every acyclic object immediately.

options.text: Memory is freed at the same rate, because Python's GC is only for statistics
options.explanation: The cycle collector does real freeing. Without it, cycles accumulate.

options.text: Reference counting continues; unreachable intact strong cycles can accumulate until explicitly collected or broken
options.explanation: Correct. gc.disable() disables automatic collection, but gc.collect() still works.

options.text: CPython switches to tracing collection instead
options.explanation: It does not switch algorithms. Automatic cyclic collection stops, while counting and explicit collection remain available.

questions.workedExample: gc.disable() disables automatic cyclic collection. Acyclic objects can still be released by reference counting; intact unreachable strong cycles can accumulate. Explicit gc.collect() works even while automatic collection is disabled. Breaking links can also remove cycles. gc.freeze() is a different API that excludes existing tracked objects from future collections until unfrozen.

questions.prompt: Why does Rust provide both `Rc<T>` and `Arc<T>`?

options.text: `Rc` is for the stack and `Arc` is for the heap
options.explanation: Both allocate their value and counts on the heap. The difference is thread safety.

options.text: `Arc` can collect cycles and `Rc` cannot
options.explanation: Neither collects cycles. Both need `Weak` to break them.

options.text: `Rc` counts references and `Arc` traces them
options.explanation: Both are reference counted; the A stands for atomic.

options.text: `Rc` uses plain increments and is single-threaded only; `Arc` uses atomic counts so it can be shared between threads
options.explanation: Correct. Non-atomic counts are cheaper, and the compiler stops you sending an `Rc` to another thread (it is not `Send`), so you only pay for atomics when you need them.

questions.workedExample:
1. A reference count is a shared counter.
2. If two threads increment it with a plain `count += 1` at the same time, one update can be lost, leading to a premature free.
3. Atomic instructions prevent that but cost more.
4. Rust lets you choose:

| Type | Count | Threads |
|---|---|---|
| `Rc` | plain | one |
| `Arc` | atomic | many |

5. The type system enforces the choice at compile time, so using `Rc` across threads is an error, not a race.

Arc makes reference counting thread-safe, not arbitrary payload access. Arc<T> is Send/Sync only under the corresponding T bounds; Arc<RefCell<T>> does not make RefCell thread-safe.
